item.description:
第十六章：提升影响力与收益的高级营销工具

利用联盟营销赚取丰厚收益。点击以下链接观看免费网络研讨会。

1. 浏览器插件

通过日常网站，若营销策略得当，你可以触达尽可能多的受众。然而，在某些关键业务环节上你会受到限制。没有合适的插件，你的网站只是一个静态页面。而借助插件，你可以将传播影响力提升到一个新的水平，同时改善用户体验。

虽然插件种类繁多，以下是我推荐的五款可增强联盟营销业务的插件：

Adobe Acrobat Reader

这款插件专为阅读 PDF 文件而设计。在进行某些研究时，你可能需要从电脑中获取关键的 PDF 数据。如果没有安装 Adobe Acrobat Reader 插件，你将无法阅读此类数据，这可能会妨碍你的工作进展。

你的网站上必须安装此插件。

Microsoft Silverlight

作为联盟营销人员，你的网站还应包含 Microsoft Silverlight 插件。它的功能包括运行数据库、媒体内容，以及让你的网页具有交互性。虽然它提供的服务与 Adobe Flash 类似，但微软的 Silverlight 更具优势，因为它允许用户访问一些强大的功能，如订票、观看体育直播、预订度假等。根据你的细分市场，你可以决定是否安装此插件以为网站增加更多价值。

Adobe Flash Player

这是 Adobe 推出的另一款重要插件。既然你在网站上运行营销策略，可能需要运行一些动画或 YouTube 视频来推广你的联盟产品。没有功能完善的 Adobe Flash Player，你的访问者将很难——甚至无法——观看此类教程视频。

LastPass

作为联盟营销人员，管理各种不同的密码可能相当具有挑战性。如果你与多家联盟公司合作，就需要使用不同的密码来访问这些平台。如何保证密码安全？写在笔记本上有风险，笔记本可能会丢失；如果将密码保存在手机里，手机也可能丢失。LastPass 是安全存储不同密码的最佳选择，无需担心密码落入不怀好意者之手或在使用时遗忘。

你只需安装一次插件，然后专注于业务的其他方面，无需不必要的担忧。访问任何网站时，它会自动记录你在不同网站上使用的密码以备将来使用。

Antivirus Software（防病毒软件）

你需要定期保护你的网站，抵御可能摧毁网站的外部攻击。作为防范此类恶意攻击的预防措施，你必须在网站上安装功能完善且有效的防病毒软件。这一明智的举措将帮助你持续经营，免受病毒攻击的风险。

Check My Links

对于任何网站所有者或管理员来说，这款插件是必备的。它通过扫描你的网页来帮助你维护网站上的链接，确保所有链接都能正常工作。扫描完成后，它会用红色高亮显示失效链接，以便你识别并修复它们。

Approach

我之前讨论过电子邮件营销对联盟营销人员的好处。在吸引更多流量的诱惑下，可以将此插件添加到你的网站。安装后，你将自动注册一个联系表单。Approach 本身是一个零月费的自动回复系统，提供电子邮件营销活动服务。注册后，你可以受益于以下功能：自动化社交媒体管理、无限制广播、数据安全以及免费安装。除此之外，它还通过电子邮件营销及其附带的好处支持你的业务。

这些插件也被称为"附加组件"（add-ons）和"扩展程序"（extensions）。在你的网站上安装这些插件所带来的潜在好处使其值得在你的网站上部署。当你的网站具备所有合适的工具并受到良好的保护免受攻击时，你将能够长期经营。

2. 高级关键词搜索

撰写产品评测文章时，进行关键词搜索研究至关重要——了解应在内容中包含哪些特定关键词，以提高文章在搜索引擎中的排名。有一些适合初学者的简单关键词研究技巧。然而，在这里，我将专注于高级关键词搜索，以提升你的文章在搜索引擎中的表现。

要进行有效的高级关键词搜索，有多种技巧可供使用。你可以访问此链接阅读超过 30 种进行高效高级关键词搜索的技巧。

3. 编写 PPC 广告

PPC 是 Pay-Per-Click（按点击付费）的缩写。这是一种营销技术，广告主在有人点击其广告时提供经济补偿。这是一种向你的网站引导付费流量的间接方式，而非等待可能来之不易的自然流量。

PPC 的成功取决于广告文案。这对于缺乏写作创意的人来说是一个挑战。PPC 对成功的联盟营销业务的重要性，使得联盟营销人员必须学习运行设计精良且相关性强的 PPC 广告活动的必要技能。能推出吸引人广告的广告主将因搜索引擎降低费用而受益，这种降低将增加他们的收入。用户越觉得你的引导有吸引力，Google 和其他搜索引擎在你广告被点击时向你收取的费用就越低。

item.title: What is Buddhism?
item.description: An introduction to the core concepts of Buddhism and its relevance today.

Day 1: Abundant Everything, Empty Something

We solved bread. We forgot meaning. And now nobody can figure out why we’re all so tired.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Philosophy #ModernLife #Mindfulness

Life looks fine, I guess. Job’s okay. Money’s not bad. Group chat stays busy enough.

But late at night. You know that moment? When everything’s finally quiet and there’s nothing to distract you. That’s when it shows up. Not a crisis exactly. Not sadness. It’s more like… something’s off. Something missing. And you can’t even put your finger on what.

Day 2: The Empty Pews

Churches are emptying. Fast. But the people leaving aren’t atheists — and that’s way more interesting than anyone expected.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Spirituality #Religion #ModernLife

Pews are getting emptier.

  1. 78% of Americans called themselves Christian. Last year? 55%. That’s nearly a quarter of the faithful has gone in twenty years.

Here’s what gets me to think. People didn’t suddenly decide there is no God. They decided Sunday morning had nothing to do with the rest of their week. And if you’ve ever sat through a sermon while your mind was on your mortgage… you kind of get it.

Day 3: Buddhism — Probably Not What You Think

When most people hear “Buddhism,” what comes to mind has almost nothing to do with the real thing. Here’s what it actually is.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Philosophy #History #Mindfulness

Say the word “Buddhism.”

What shows up? Incense. Shaved heads. Chanting. Old ladies bowing to golden statues. Maybe “Buddha-like youth” if you follow Chinese pop culture — the whole “whatever, nothing matters, just lie down” aesthetic.

Day 4: The Four Truths — Or, Four Discoveries That Aren’t As Bleak As They Sound

“Life is suffering.” It’s Buddhism’s most famous line. And also its most misunderstood. The word he actually used means something surprisingly different.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Philosophy #Psychology #FourNobleTruths

“Life is suffering.”

That’s the line everyone knows. And honestly, a lot of people hear that, go “well that’s depressing,” and check out. I don’t blame them. If someone walked up to me and said life is fundamentally miserable, I’d probably walk the other way too.

Day 5: Where Suffering Comes From — Three Engines You Never Noticed

Greed, hatred, delusion. They sound like moral judgments. They’re not. They’re three automatic processes running in the background. All the time.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Psychology #Mindfulness #Suffering

Last time I said suffering has causes. Not vague causes. Specific ones. Buddhism names three: greed, hatred, delusion.

Those words sound like someone wagging a finger. “You’re too greedy. You’re too angry. You’re too ignorant.” That’s not what they mean. They describe processes. Mechanical things your mind does whether you want it to or not.

Day 6: Can It Actually Stop? — What Nirvana Really Means

Nirvana. The word conjures monks in lotus position, permanently checked out from reality. That’s not it. It means something way more useful.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Philosophy #Nirvana #Freedom

Nirvana might be Buddhism’s most badly handled word in English.

The image most people have: a monk meditating forever, eyes closed, never moving again. Or some abstract nothingness. A void. The permanent off switch.

Day 7: The Map — Eight Dimensions, One Path

If there’s a way out, what does it look like? Buddhism draws a map. Eight landmarks. Not rules. Training dimensions.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #EightfoldPath #Practice #Overview

Six days of problem. Today: the solution.

Buddhism calls it the Eightfold Path. The name makes it sound like eight separate roads. It’s not. Think of it as eight sides of one thing. Eight dimensions you can start training — any of them, all of them, right now.

Day 8: Who Was the Buddha, Actually?

Not a god. Not a prophet. A guy who saw something he couldn’t un-see, walked away from everything, and figured out how to look at his own mind.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #History #Buddha #Philosophy

Week two. We’re pulling the camera back. Last week was the framework. This week: how the whole thing happened. Where it came from. Who started it.

So. Siddhartha Gautama. Northern India. Himalayas. 2,600 years ago.

Day 9: The Soil — What the Buddha Inherited

The Buddha didn’t appear out of nowhere. He stood on two thousand years of Indian thought. And then broke from almost all of it.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #History #IndianPhilosophy #Karma

The Buddha didn’t invent Buddhism from scratch. Nobody invents anything from scratch.

Before him, India already had two thousand years of philosophical accumulation. Three major currents. The Buddha drew from all of them, and then — this is the interesting part — broke from each one in a different way.

Day 10: After the Buddha — The First Split

The Buddha dies. His students panic. Who decides what the teachings mean? The answer creates a crack that runs through all of Buddhist history.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #History #Schism #Theravada

Most people picture Buddhism as one unified thing. Same texts, same rules, same beliefs, forever. Not even close.

Buddhism split within a century of its founder’s death. And this wasn’t some accident. It was practically guaranteed by the way he set things up.

Day 11: The Mahayana Revolution — From “Save Myself” to “Save Everyone”

Early Buddhism was built for individual liberation. Then someone asked: what if it was for everyone? The biggest pivot in Buddhist history.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Mahayana #History #Bodhisattva

After the first split, Buddhism settled into two camps. The Sthavira (elders) and the Mahasanghika (the majority). But the real earthquake hadn’t happened yet.

Around the 1st century BCE to 1st century CE, new texts started appearing. They claimed to be the Buddha’s words — but their content was radically different from anything that came before. These texts announced the biggest internal revolution in the history of any religion: Mahayana Buddhism.

Day 12: When Buddhism Met Daoism — The First Contact

67 CE. A Chinese emperor dreams of a golden man. Two Indian monks arrive on white horses. Buddhism enters China. Nobody understands a word of it.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Daoism #ChineseHistory #Geyi

Year 67 CE. Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han has a dream. A golden figure, glowing, floating through his palace.

The next morning he asks his ministers. One says: there’s a sage in the west. They call him “Buddha.”

Day 13: Bodhidharma’s Wall — Chan Is Born

An Indian monk arrives in China. Meets the emperor. Says “no merit.” Crosses a river on a reed. Faces a wall for nine years. And doesn’t say a word.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Bodhidharma #Huineng #History

Around 520 CE. A monk from India arrives by sea at Guangzhou. He’s supposedly over a hundred years old. His mission, as later tradition tells it: find one person “who won’t be deceived.”

Day 14: Four Words — The Chan Manifesto

“Not depending on words. A special transmission outside teachings. Direct pointing at mind. See your nature, become Buddha.” Sixteen words. The whole thing.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Zen #Philosophy #DirectExperience

Chan describes itself in four phrases. Sixteen Chinese characters. This is the manifesto.

Not established on words. A special transmission outside the teachings. Direct pointing at the human mind. See your nature, become Buddha.

Day 15: The Platform Sutra — The Only Chinese “Sutra”

In Buddhism, only the Buddha’s words are called “sutras.” One exception. Spoken by an illiterate woodcutter from Guangdong. Why has it survived 1,300 years?

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #PlatformSutra #Huineng #ChinesePhilosophy

In Buddhism, a “sutra” is the highest category of text. Reserved for the Buddha’s actual words. Thousands of Buddhist books exist across India, China, Tibet, Japan. Almost none of them get called sutras.

Day 16: Sudden vs. Gradual — Can Freedom Arrive in One Step?

Five generations of Chan masters built the gradual path. Huineng walked in and said: you can skip it. Who was right?

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Huineng #Shenxiu #Enlightenment

The Fifth Patriarch, Hongren, wanted someone to succeed him. He told the monks: write a verse. Show me your understanding.

The senior disciple, Shenxiu, had the learning, the reputation, the support of the whole monastery. Everyone expected him to win. He wrote:

Day 17: No-Thought, No-Form, No-Abiding — Three Definitions of Mental Freedom

Three words from the Platform Sutra. They sound like mysticism. They’re actually an operations manual you can test today.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Huineng #Mindfulness #MentalFreedom

Huineng gave Chan (Zen)¹ a three-word definition of what a free mind looks like: no-thought, no-form, no-abiding. These aren’t philosophy. They’re more like a recipe. You can try them. They’ll either work or they won’t.

Day 18: Koans — Not Riddles. Mental Training Tools.

“Does a dog have Buddha-nature?” Zhaozhou: “No!” Not a puzzle. Not a trick. A tool designed to break your favorite tool: interpretation.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Koans #Zhaozhou #Psychology

Yesterday was the manual. No-thought, no-form, no-abiding. Today is the exercise book.

Chan (Zen)¹ invented something called gong’an — public cases. More commonly known by the Japanese pronunciation: koans. A monk asks a question. The master responds. Usually it’s baffling. Sometimes it’s hitting someone.

Day 19: Everyday Chan — Practice Doesn’t Happen on the Cushion

“Carrying water, chopping wood — nothing but the wondrous Way.” The most radical thing Chan ever said: your whole life is practice. Including the boring parts.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Mazu #Baizhang #EverydayLife

In Indian Buddhism, practice and ordinary life were separate things. You wanted to practice? Shave your head. Put on robes. Leave home. Go to the forest or the monastery. Cities are noise. People are distraction. Only by leaving all of it can the mind settle.

Day 20: Chan and Daoism — When Zhuangzi Met Huineng

Two traditions, separated by a thousand years. One gave the seed. The other built the map. Where they overlap is fascinating. Where they split is more useful.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Daoism #Zhuangzi #ChinesePhilosophy

Chan (Zen)¹ is Chinese. But it’s not “pure” Chinese — it’s what happens when Indian Buddhism flows into the Daoist river. Two currents, merged.

Today I want to look at the upstream source: Zhuangzi. You’ll see Chan’s shadow in him. Or maybe you’ll see Zhuangzi’s bones under Chan’s skin. Depends how you look.

Day 21: Chan and Confucianism — How to Be in the World Without Being of It

Confucianism says: engage. Chan says: let go. They look like enemies. What Chinese monks actually built between them is smarter than either side alone.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Confucianism #Huineng #Dahui

Last day of Week 3. The final dialogue partner.

Confucianism and Chan (Zen)¹ sit at opposite ends of the Chinese thought spectrum.

Confucianism: cultivate yourself, manage your family, govern the state, bring peace to the world. Throw yourself into life. Be useful to others. Your relationships are your path.

Day 22: The Knowing-Doing Gap

Why you understand the theory but still snap at your partner

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Practice #Self-Awareness #Habit

Today’s Chan Line “Before enlightenment, chop wood, carry water. After enlightenment, chop wood, carry water.” The doing doesn’t change. What changes is who’s doing it. And there’s no shortcut to that change.

I’ve read thirty books on Buddhism. Maybe forty. I can explain the Five Aggregates at a dinner party. I can draw you a diagram of dependent origination on a napkin.

Day 23: Watching the Breath

A two-minute exercise nobody can fail

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Meditation #Breath #Practice

Today’s Chan Line “The mind is like a wild ox. Tie it to the post of the breath.” You don’t tame the ox by yelling at it. You tie the rope and wait. The breath is the post.

Most meditation instructions are too long.

I mean this. I’ve read instructions that run three pages before you even sit down. Posture. Cushion height. Hand position. Tongue placement. Eyes open or closed. By the time you finish reading, you’ve already failed — because now meditation is a thing you read about instead of a thing you do.

Day 24: Eating, Walking, Talking

Mindfulness doesn’t need a cushion

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Mindfulness #DailyLife #Practice

Today’s Chan Line “In carrying water, in chopping wood — this is the wonderful Way.” The ordinary is not an obstacle to practice. It’s the only practice there is.

Yesterday I gave you a sitting exercise. Today is the opposite: practice while moving.

Here’s the problem with meditation. It cordons off “spiritual time” from “real time.” You sit for ten minutes. Then you stand up and the rest of your day is unchanged. The practice stays on the cushion.

Day 25: When Emotions Hit

Anger is not your enemy. Your autopilot is.

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Emotions #Anger #Mindfulness

Today’s Chan Line “If you want to tread the path of the Buddha, don’t seek outside. When a thought of anger arises, just see it.” The seeing is enough. You don’t need to fix it. You need to notice it before it notices you.

I used to think Buddhism wanted me to stop feeling angry. Like the goal was this placid, unshakeable calm where nothing bothered me. A kind of emotional flatline.

Day 26: Buddhism in Relationships

The person you love is also the hardest practice

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Relationships #Compassion #Mettā

Today’s Chan Line “A bodhisattva does not abandon any living being. Not because it’s easy. Because that’s the work.” Compassion is not a feeling. It’s a direction you keep pointing toward — especially when you don’t want to.

Sitting alone in a quiet room is one thing. Sitting across from someone who just said something unfair about you — that’s the real training ground.

Day 27: Impermanence and Death

The thing you’re avoiding is the only exit

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Impermanence #Death #Anicca

Today’s Chan Line “All conditioned things are impermanent. Work out your liberation with diligence.” The Buddha’s last words. No poetry. No consolation. Just: this is how things are. Now practice.

I don’t want to write this one.

That’s probably exactly why I should. Death is the topic Buddhism is most known for and the topic most of us — including me — least want to look at directly. We dress it up. We philosophize. We do everything except sit with the fact that we’re going to die, and so is everyone we love, and there’s no loophole.

Day 28: Buddhism and Psychology

The clinicians and the monks found the same thing from different directions

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Psychology #CBT #ACT #MBSR

Today’s Chan Line “The mind is originally pure. Defilement is adventitious.” The Platform Sutra. Twelve centuries later, cognitive therapy arrives at the same insight: thoughts are not facts. They’re events. They pass.

This one surprised me when I first dug into it. I assumed Buddhism and psychology were parallel but separate tracks — one spiritual, one clinical. Turns out they’ve been in conversation for decades, and the overlap isn’t vague. It’s specific. Testable. Published in journals.

Day 29: The 30-Day Map

Four questions and twenty-eight answers

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Zen #Review #Practice

Today’s Chan Line “The finger pointing at the moon is not the moon.” This entire series is a finger. Don’t mistake it for what it’s pointing at. But don’t ignore the finger either.

Twenty-eight days. Twenty-eight attempts to say something true about a tradition that’s spent 2,500 years insisting that truth can’t be said.

Day 30: Your Next Steps

The map is not the road

Tags: #Buddhism #Chan #Zen #Practice #Reading

Today’s Chan Line “Before I had studied Chan for thirty years, I saw mountains as mountains, and rivers as rivers. When I arrived at a more intimate knowledge, I saw that mountains are not mountains and rivers are not rivers. But now that I have got its very substance, I am at rest. For it’s just that I see mountains once again as mountains, and rivers once again as rivers.” — Qingyuan Weixin The endpoint looks like the beginning. But it’s not.
